name: Discrete-time survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards

identity.method_name: Discrete-time (person-period) hazard models -- complementary log-log or logistic link -- and the continuous-time Cox (1972) proportional hazards model; extended by Random Survival Forest (Ishwaran et al. 2008) and concordance-index-optimised gradient boosting (Chen, Jia, Mercola, Xie 2013, 'GBMCI')
identity.core_idea: Reframes 'predictive risk analysis' as time-to-event modelling: instead of predicting a static encroachment score per lake-year, the model estimates the hazard -- the conditional probability that a lake crosses an encroachment threshold in year t, given it has not crossed it in any earlier year. Discrete-time hazard models fit a standard binary regression (logit or complementary log-log link) on data reshaped into one row per lake per year-at-risk (a 'person-period', here 'lake-period', table), which is the exact shape of the project's existing 42-row lake-year table. Cox proportional hazards instead treats time as continuous and models the hazard as a baseline hazard multiplied by exp(linear predictor), estimated via partial likelihood using only the ORDERING of event times, not their absolute values. Random Survival Forest and concordance-index-boosted gradient boosting are machine-learning generalisations that relax the proportional-hazards linearity assumption but still fundamentally require a reasonable number of observed events to learn any signal, exactly as the linear models do.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. This is a statistical modelling framework, not a dataset; it would be applied to the project's own 42-row lake-year table (6 lakes x 7 years), reshaped into person-period (lake-period) format.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Threshold rule, and a circular one unless deliberately isolated from the project's own detection method. There is no confirmed 'this lake was encroached in year t' record for any lake (project_constraints.ground_truth: None), so the survival outcome (the event indicator) has to be manufactured from the same proxy metrics the project already computes -- e.g. 'water area fell below X% of its 2019 baseline' or 'built-up-within-buffer area exceeded Y hectares'. If that threshold is the same MNDWI/NDVI rule used as the current baseline method, then 'fitting a hazard model to it' is restating the existing rule's timing in a different mathematical language, not adding new evidence. A non-circular version would require the event to be anchored to an external source (e.g. a Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority enforcement record, a Bengaluru Development Authority notice, or a dated satellite-verified construction start) -- none of which exist for any of the 6 lakes per project_constraints.ground_truth. Cost: near-zero to define a circular threshold-based event (hours); realistically unbounded (months to years, outside student scope) to obtain even one externally verified encroachment onset date per lake.
fit_to_project.input_required: A person-period (lake-period) table: one row per lake per year the lake remains 'at risk' (has not yet had the event), with an event indicator (0/1) and covariates for that year. The event indicator and its timing are NOT already available -- they must be constructed from the proxy metrics described above, since no confirmed onset date exists for any lake.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: no, for any covariate-adjusted model. The lake-year table already matches the required person-period shape (no reframing needed, unlike the pixel-based DL items), but the number of independent subjects for survival inference is not 42, it is 6 (the lakes); years are repeated measurements within each subject, not new independent units. Worse, the number of OBSERVED EVENTS -- not the number of rows -- is what determines whether any hazard model is estimable, and with a plausible, honest event definition applied to only 6 lakes over 7 years, the realistic count is zero or one lake ever crossing a defined threshold within the observation window. A model with zero events cannot be fit at all (the Cox partial likelihood and the discrete-time binomial likelihood both require at least one event to contribute any information); a model with exactly one event can be technically fit but is statistically meaningless (see events-per-variable below). A purely descriptive Kaplan-Meier-equivalent survival curve with no covariates could in principle be drawn, but with 0-1 events it would show either a flat 100%-survival line (uninformative) or a single vertical drop with no basis for a confidence band.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels, and the weak label here is unusually fragile: unlike a classifier where a wrong label degrades one prediction, a wrong or circular EVENT DEFINITION in survival analysis fabricates the entire outcome variable that every downstream hazard ratio, C-index and survival curve is computed from. There is no version of this method that works with zero labels.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Not a resolution-dependent method in the pixel sense -- it operates on lake-year aggregate features (e.g. percentage water area, percentage built-up area within a buffer) that are already derived from the project's 20 m Sentinel-2 grid and rolled up to one number per lake-year, so there is no foreign-resolution pretrained-model mismatch to flag here.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: An event indicator and event-year per lake. Absent an external source, this must come from the project's own spectral or building thresholds, which is exactly the circularity problem above; 'none' is not an option since every survival model requires a defined event.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Directly reframes limitation (3) (no real ground truth) into a precise, checkable statement -- 'we have zero or one observed events, so no hazard model is estimable' is itself a valuable, honest finding rather than a fix. It does not fix limitation (1) (42 rows); if anything it exposes that the effective sample size for this kind of inference is 6 lakes, not 42 rows, which is worse than the tabular framing suggests. It does not fix limitation (2) (OpenStreetMap buildings are a single 2026 snapshot, so a 'building growth' covariate would be time-invariant across all 7 person-periods of a given lake, contributing nothing to a time-varying hazard). It does not fix limitation (4) (still one dry-season scene per year feeding each lake-period row).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. Whatever proxy threshold defines the 'event' inherits the desilting confound completely: Bellandur's water area going 15.7 ha (2019) -> 0.4 ha (2021) -> 107.9 ha (2025) would, under a naive water-area-loss event definition, register a hazard 'event' in 2021 and then an impossible 'un-event' in 2025, which no standard survival model (non-recurring event, single failure per subject) can represent without an ad hoc competing-risks or recurrent-event extension -- and building that extension does not resolve whether the underlying spectral signal means encroachment or maintenance dredging; that has to be resolved before the event indicator is built, not by the survival model itself.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No. If the event is defined via a vegetation-area threshold (e.g. 'vegetation area within the lake footprint exceeded Z hectares'), Bellandur's and Varthur's water-hyacinth mats (Bellandur 2019: 16 ha water vs 260 ha vegetation inside a 315 ha footprint) would trigger a false 'event' driven by a floating macrophyte bloom, not construction. The published Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover mapping (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843) could in principle be used to clean the vegetation signal BEFORE constructing the event indicator, but that is a pre-processing fix to the confound, not something the hazard model contributes.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None inherently. The hazard being modelled ('crossing an encroachment threshold') is only as legally grounded as whatever threshold defines it. If the event were anchored to the 30 m Master Plan buffer (as reinstated by the Supreme Court) or the earlier 75 m National Green Tribunal buffer -- i.e. 'built-up footprint inside the buffer exceeded some area' -- that would be a more legally motivated choice of buffer than a raw water-area threshold, but the building layer feeding it is the single, static 2026 OpenStreetMap snapshot (project_constraints.building_data), so no year-by-year 'crossing' can ever actually be observed from that data source; this is a dead end tied directly to limitation (2).
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: This is the one place in the project where the required data shape (one row per lake-year) matches the method's natural unit exactly, so no artificial reframing is needed. However, any covariate drawn from OpenStreetMap buildings is time-invariant across all 7 lake-periods of a given lake and therefore cannot explain WHY an event happens in one particular year rather than another (it can only appear as a fixed, non-informative lake-level offset). Covariates drawn from the annual Sentinel-2 scene (water/vegetation index values) do genuinely vary year to year, but they are typically the very same quantities used to define the event, which risks a tautological hazard rather than a predictive one.

implementation.libraries: lifelines (CoxPHFitter, KaplanMeierFitter, NelsonAalenFitter) for the continuous-time Cox model and descriptive survival curves; scikit-survival (sksurv.ensemble.RandomSurvivalForest, sksurv.linear_model.CoxPHSurvivalAnalysis, sksurv.ensemble.GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis) for Random Survival Forest and boosted survival models; statsmodels (GLM with a Binomial family and cloglog link, or plain logit) or scikit-learn LogisticRegression on the manually reshaped person-period table for discrete-time hazard models; PyDTS (a newer, purpose-built Python package for discrete-time survival analysis with competing risks) as an alternative to hand-rolling the person-period reshape.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable. All of these are fit from scratch on the project's own lake-period table; there are no pretrained weights for a Cox model, a discrete-time hazard model, a Random Survival Forest, or GBMCI-style boosting to import.
implementation.licence: lifelines is MIT licensed. scikit-survival is GPL-3.0 licensed [verify -- confirm current licence on the scikit-survival GitHub repository before relying on this for any redistribution decision]. statsmodels is BSD-3-Clause. All are usable in an academic project; scikit-survival's copyleft licence only matters if the project intends to redistribute modified library code, which a capstone project normally would not.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial. Fitting any of these models to a 42-row (or smaller, once reshaped to person-periods) table takes well under a second on a laptop CPU; no GPU is needed at any point. This is among the cheapest computational items in the entire project outline -- the cost of this item is entirely in deciding what the event even is, not in fitting the model.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 2-4 student-days to implement the pipeline end to end (person-period reshape, fitting lifelines/scikit-survival models, producing Kaplan-Meier and Cox output) -- but this estimate is almost irrelevant, because the honest conclusion (see risk/verdict) is reached almost immediately once the event count is tallied. The real time sink, if pursued past the feasibility check, is arguing for a non-circular event definition, which is open-ended and not bounded by a student-days estimate.

evaluation.metrics: Harrell's concordance index (C-index) or Uno's C for censoring-robust discrimination, integrated Brier score for calibration, and time-dependent AUC; for discrete-time hazard models, per-interval hazard estimates and their standard errors. All of these metrics are either undefined or degenerate when there are zero events, and are estimated from a vanishingly small number of comparable pairs when there is exactly one event (see leakage_risk).
evaluation.validation_protocol: Leave-one-lake-out is the only defensible split, since the subject of inference is the lake (6 independent clusters), not the lake-year row; a naive random split on the 42 lake-year rows would place different years of the same lake in both train and test, leaking that lake's entire survival trajectory. Note the mechanical problem this creates: with a maximum of 0-1 total events across 6 lakes, at least 5 of the 6 leave-one-lake-out folds are guaranteed to train on zero events, and the remaining fold may or may not contain the single event -- there is no split of this data that gives every fold a non-degenerate training set.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Three concrete risks, one of which is specific to survival modelling: (1) the standard same-lake-across-years leakage described above; (2) definitional leakage/circularity -- if the event indicator is derived from the same spectral index used as a covariate, the model is fit to predict its own definition, and any reported concordance index is close to tautological; (3) concordance-index degeneracy -- Harrell's C-index is computed only over 'comparable pairs' (an observed event compared against subjects still at risk at that time); with 6 lakes and at most 1 event, the number of comparable pairs is at most 5, so any C-index reported from this data has enormous sampling variance and is not a stable estimate of discriminative ability, regardless of which model produced it.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: Cox and discrete-time hazard models report asymptotic standard errors and confidence intervals, but asymptotic theory assumes many events, not zero or one; at this event count, reported confidence intervals would be uninformatively wide or (with zero events) simply not computable, since the partial likelihood has no curvature to invert for a variance estimate. Bootstrap resampling does not rescue this: resampling 6 clusters with 0-1 events will frequently produce bootstrap replicates with zero events, for which the hazard is undefined, so a bootstrap confidence interval built from a mixture of computable and non-computable replicates is not a valid interval. This is exactly the gap conformal prediction (item C7 in this same outline) is built to fill for a small-n point estimate, though conformal prediction does not solve the deeper problem that the underlying event label is itself proxy-derived.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Directly applicable and high-risk if attempted: because the honest event count is 0-1, there would be a strong temptation to synthetically generate additional lake-years, simulate plausible event times, or relax the event definition until more 'events' appear. Any of these would fabricate an encroachment-timing signal that does not exist in the verified data and must be explicitly disclosed as synthetic if used at all; the defensible response to a near-zero event count is to report the null result, not to manufacture events to make the model fittable.

evidence.published_performance: Chen, Jia, Mercola and Xie (2013), 'A Gradient Boosting Algorithm for Survival Analysis via Direct Optimization of Concordance Index', Computational and Mathematical Methods in Medicine, doi 10.1155/2013/873595 (PMC3853154) -- note that the DOI given in the task brief, 10.1371/journal.pone.0079269, resolves to an unrelated PLOS ONE developmental-biology paper on holoprosencephaly in mice, not this survival paper; PMC3853154 / doi 10.1155/2013/873595 is the correct identifier and is used throughout this file. That paper reports their GBMCI method achieving concordance indices of roughly 0.66-0.74 [verify] on the METABRIC breast-cancer cohort (1,981 patients, split 1,001 training / 980 testing, with several hundred observed deaths), outperforming standard Cox regression, boosted Cox and Random Survival Forest on that dataset. Ishwaran et al. (2008), 'Random Survival Forests', Annals of Applied Statistics 2(3):841-860, is the foundational RSF reference and reports strong discrimination on multiple clinical datasets with hundreds to thousands of subjects and substantial event counts [verify exact figures against the primary source]. None of these performance figures are transferable to this project: they were obtained with two to three orders of magnitude more subjects and events than 6 lakes and 0-1 events can ever provide.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Clinical oncology (METABRIC breast cancer cohort, UK/Canada, ~2,000 patients) for GBMCI; multiple clinical and biomedical cohorts, again with hundreds-to-thousands of subjects and rich event counts, for Random Survival Forest. No environmental, remote-sensing or land-cover application of comparable scale to 6 lakes was found.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No application of discrete-time survival analysis, Cox proportional hazards, Random Survival Forest, or concordance-index-boosted survival models to Indian urban lakes, Bengaluru lakes, or lake/wetland encroachment anywhere was found in the literature search performed for this item. If pursued, this would be a genuinely novel application with no precedent to calibrate feasibility expectations against, which cuts both ways: no prior failure to point to, but also no prior success.
evidence.evidence_recency: Foundational theory ranges from Cox (1972, proportional hazards) and Peduzzi et al. (1996, events-per-variable rule) through Singer and Willett (1993, discrete-time survival via logistic/person-period models) to Ishwaran et al. (2008, Random Survival Forest) and Chen et al. (2013, GBMCI); per the brief's own carve-out, pre-2020 dates are acceptable for core statistical theory. The most recent supporting evidence found (PyDTS package, arXiv 2204.05731) is from 2022, so the framework as a whole is actively maintained, not abandoned.
evidence.primary_sources: Cox, D.R. (1972), 'Regression Models and Life-Tables', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 34(2):187-220; Singer, J.D. and Willett, J.B. (1993), 'It's About Time: Using Discrete-Time Survival Analysis to Study Duration and the Timing of Events', Journal of Educational Statistics 18(2), https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/10769986018002155; Peduzzi, P., Concato, J., Kemper, E., Holford, T.R., Feinstein, A.R. (1996), 'A simulation study of the number of events per variable in logistic regression analysis', Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 49(12):1373-9; Vittinghoff, E. and McCulloch, C.E. (2007), 'Relaxing the Rule of Ten Events per Variable in Logistic and Cox Regression', American Journal of Epidemiology 165(6):710-8, https://academic.oup.com/aje/article-abstract/165/6/710/63906; Ishwaran, H., Kogalur, U.B., Blackstone, E.H., Lauer, M.S. (2008), 'Random Survival Forests', Annals of Applied Statistics 2(3):841-860; Chen, Y., Jia, Z., Mercola, D., Xie, X. (2013), 'A Gradient Boosting Algorithm for Survival Analysis via Direct Optimization of Concordance Index', Computational and Mathematical Methods in Medicine 2013:873595, doi 10.1155/2013/873595, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3853154/; lifelines documentation, https://lifelines.readthedocs.io/; scikit-survival documentation, https://scikit-survival.readthedocs.io/; PyDTS, arXiv:2204.05731, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.05731.

risk.failure_modes: (1) Zero observed events: the Cox partial likelihood and the discrete-time binomial/cloglog likelihood are both flat with no events, so no coefficient can be estimated at all -- the model literally does not fit, it errors or returns undefined output. (2) One observed event: technically fittable but statistically meaningless -- events-per-variable (EPV) of 1 is far below even the most relaxed published thresholds (Vittinghoff and McCulloch's relaxation still assumes roughly 5-9 EPV as a floor, not 1), so any fitted coefficient, hazard ratio or concordance index is dominated by sampling noise from a single data point and cannot be trusted for inference. (3) Random Survival Forest and GBMCI both build many bootstrap-resampled trees/iterations; with at most 1 event in the full data, most bootstrap resamples will contain zero events, making the log-rank-based split criterion (RSF) or the pairwise concordance loss (GBMCI) undefined or degenerate for the majority of the ensemble, so the ensemble degrades toward an uninformative random partition rather than a trained model. (4) Every leave-one-lake-out fold removes one of only 6 lakes, so at least 5 of 6 folds train on zero events regardless of which model family is used -- there is no valid cross-validation split of this data. (5) Censoring is not cleanly defined: standard right-censoring means 'we know the subject had not yet had the event as of the last observation', which presumes we can reliably determine non-occurrence of the event -- but per project_constraints.ground_truth there is no confirmed encroachment status for any lake in any year, so 'not yet encroached' is itself an inference from the same noisy, confounded proxy metrics (desilting and hyacinth included) that produce the event indicator in the first place. This is a strictly harder problem than ordinary censoring, where the difficulty is only in the TIMING of a well-defined event, not in whether the event occurred at all.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask, almost immediately, 'how many lakes actually had a confirmed encroachment event, and when?' If the honest answer is zero or one, then presenting any fitted hazard ratio, survival curve with a confidence band, or concordance index as a substantive result is not defensible -- it would be presenting a number computed from an underdetermined or degenerate likelihood as if it carried information. The defensible response is to present this item as a formal feasibility analysis: state the events-per-variable requirement, tally the actual event count from whatever proxy definition is used, show that the requirement is not met by roughly an order of magnitude, and state explicitly what would be needed to make the analysis viable (on the order of 10+ lakes with confirmed, dated encroachment onset, i.e. an events-per-variable-compliant dataset that does not currently exist and cannot be built within a one-student capstone). This turns a vague aspiration in the project title into a named, checkable, and honestly negative finding, which is itself defensible; presenting a fitted number without this caveat is not.
risk.honest_expectation: The realistic, reportable outcome of this item is a null result: discrete-time survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards CANNOT be credibly estimated on 6 lakes with 7 years and zero-to-one observed events, and this should be stated plainly rather than worked around. The value delivered is not a working hazard model but (a) a precise, citable statistical name for what 'predictive risk analysis' was vaguely gesturing at, (b) an explicit, referenced sample-size/event-count argument (the events-per-variable rule) explaining exactly why it fails here, and (c) a clear statement of what data collection would be required to make it viable in a future iteration of the project. A demonstration fit (e.g. attempting lifelines' CoxPHFitter on the honestly-labelled data and showing it fails to converge or returns a coefficient with a standard error orders of magnitude larger than the coefficient itself) is a legitimate, low-cost way to document this due diligence.

verdict.recommended_rank: reject as a working predictive model; adopt-if-time as a documented feasibility/null-result section -- the value here is entirely in naming the framework and showing, with the events-per-variable rule, exactly why it cannot be estimated on this data, not in producing a fitted hazard model.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We investigated discrete-time survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards as the formal statistical framework behind 'predictive risk analysis', but with only 6 lakes and zero-to-one observed encroachment events (against a rule-of-thumb requirement of roughly 10 events per covariate), no hazard model is estimable here, and we report that as a specific, citable limitation rather than fitting and presenting an unreliable number.
